title: How to read a recipe before you start
summary: The five minutes that prevent most kitchen panic.
body:
Read the whole recipe start to finish before you touch a pan. It sounds obvious and almost nobody does it, and it's the single biggest difference between cooking calmly and cooking in a panic.

You're looking for three things.

- Hidden waiting. "Marinate for 2 hours" or "chill overnight" buried in step 3 will wreck your evening if you find it at 7pm.
- Steps that overlap. If the sauce simmers for 20 minutes, that's when you prep everything else — not after.
- Things you don't have. Both ingredients and equipment. A recipe that needs a blender at step 6 is worth knowing about at step 0.

Then do what restaurants call mise en place: get every ingredient measured and every vegetable cut before any heat goes on. Once you're cooking, things move faster than you can chop.

One more habit worth building: recipe times are optimistic. They usually measure the cooking, not the peeling, and they assume you already know the steps. Add half again for a dish you've never made.

title: Holding a knife without fear
summary: Grip, the claw, and why a sharp knife is the safe one.
body:
Grip the handle where it meets the blade and pinch the blade itself between thumb and forefinger. It feels wrong for about a day and then feels like the only sensible way to hold a knife — you get far more control than gripping the handle alone.

Your other hand makes the claw. Curl your fingertips under so your knuckles face the blade, and let the flat of the knife rest against those knuckles as you cut. The knuckles guide the blade and your fingertips are tucked out of reach. This is the whole trick to not cutting yourself.

Don't chop by lifting the knife straight up and down. Push the blade forward and down, letting the curve do the work, then draw it back. Long strokes, not hacking.

- A sharp knife is safer than a blunt one. Blunt knives slide off food instead of biting into it, and that slide is where the accident happens.
- Put a damp cloth under your chopping board. A board that skids is the other common cause of cuts.
- Cut a flat side onto anything round before you do anything else, then rest it on that face. Round vegetables roll, and rolling is when you lose control.

title: Salt: when, not just how much
summary: Why seasoning as you go beats fixing it at the end.
body:
The most common thing separating home cooking from restaurant cooking isn't skill or equipment. It's that restaurants season in layers and home cooks season once at the end.

Salt added early dissolves into the food. Salt added at the end sits on the surface, so the dish tastes salty on the outside and flat underneath. Add a little at each stage — when the onions go in, when the liquid goes in, before serving — and taste each time.

- Taste constantly. This is the actual skill. You cannot season food you haven't tasted.
- Under-salt on purpose while cooking. You can always add; you can't take away.
- If something tastes dull but salty enough, it usually wants acid, not more salt. A squeeze of lemon or a splash of vinegar wakes up almost anything.

A note on salt itself: different salts are not interchangeable by volume. A teaspoon of fine table salt holds far more salt than a teaspoon of flaky sea salt, because the flakes pack loosely. If a dish comes out aggressively salty, that mismatch is often why.

title: Getting the pan hot enough
summary: Most beginner food is grey because the pan was cold.
body:
Beginner cooking is usually too timid with heat. Meat comes out grey instead of brown, vegetables steam instead of roasting, and everything sticks.

Browning is a chemical reaction that needs real heat. Below that threshold, food just releases water and sits in it. That's the difference between a seared steak and a boiled one.

How to know the pan is ready:

- Heat the pan first, then add oil, then add food. Oil into a cold pan just soaks in and smokes by the time the pan catches up.
- The oil should shimmer and move like water when you tilt the pan. If it's sitting still, wait.
- Food should sizzle audibly the instant it lands. Silence means the pan wasn't ready.

Then leave it alone. Food sticks to a hot pan at first and releases by itself once a crust forms. If you have to fight to turn it, it isn't ready to turn.

The opposite mistake is crowding. Too much food at once drops the pan temperature and everything steams in its own liquid. Cook in batches; it's faster than it looks because you're not waiting for a flooded pan to recover.

title: Cooking without a recipe
summary: A pattern that turns whatever you have into dinner.
body:
Most weeknight meals are the same shape wearing different clothes: something starchy, something green, something with protein, and something with enough flavour to tie them together.

Once you see the pattern you can build dinner from whatever's actually in the fridge instead of shopping for a specific recipe.

- Start with an aromatic base. Onion or garlic in fat, cooked gently until soft and sweet. This is the foundation of an enormous number of dishes across every cuisine.
- Add your longest-cooking ingredient next, then work down to the quickest. Root vegetables early, leafy greens last.
- Finish with something sharp and something fresh. Lemon, vinegar, yoghurt; herbs, spring onion. This is what stops a dish tasting heavy and one-note.

The direction comes from what you add to the base. Soy, ginger and sesame go one way; cumin, coriander and lemon another; garlic, tomato and basil somewhere else. Pick a lane and stay in it — most kitchen disasters are two lanes at once.

Use the Fridge tab to see what you actually have, then Browse with "Can make" to see what's already within reach.

title: Knowing when things are done
summary: Time is a guess. Look, poke, and smell instead.
body:
Recipe timings assume a specific pan, a specific hob, and food at a specific temperature. Yours are all different, so treat any time in a recipe as a rough guide and judge the food itself.

What to trust instead:

- Meat: go by firmness and juices, or use a thermometer if you have one. A thermometer removes the guesswork entirely and is the single most useful cheap kitchen tool.
- Vegetables: pierce with a knife tip. It should meet a little resistance for most things, none at all for potatoes you're going to mash.
- Pasta: taste it. Always. Start two minutes before the packet says.
- Baking: colour and smell tell you more than the timer. Things smell done just before they look done.

Carryover cooking catches people out: food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, especially large pieces of meat. Pull things slightly early and let them rest. Resting isn't optional — cutting straight into meat pushes all the juice onto the board instead of leaving it in the food.
